mdl_consolidation_status.label: RESOLVED as of August 18, 2026 -- the JPML has ruled
mdl_consolidation_status.detail: The Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation issued its transfer order on August 18, 2026 (Document 117, MDL No. 3191), centralizing the turnout-gear-only actions in the DISTRICT OF MINNESOTA before Judge Jeffrey M. Bryan -- not Montana (which the moving party and most parties had agreed to prefer at oral argument) and not South Carolina (Judge Gergel's AFFF MDL 2873, which 3M and other defendants had pushed for). The consolidated litigation is now captioned 'In re: Non-AFFF Firefighter Turnout Gear Marketing, Sales Practices, and Products Liability Litigation.' The panel explicitly drew a legal line: MDL 2873 is reserved for claims alleging direct AFFF chemical exposure/harm; these actions allege only PFAS-in-gear harm with no AFFF-exposure claim, so they get their own, separate MDL. Any future action alleging both would still go to Judge Gergel's MDL 2873.
mdl_consolidation_status.implication: This resolves the previously-unresolved venue question. Going forward, a new municipality joining this wave most likely becomes a tag-along action filed into or transferred to MDL 3191 in D. Minnesota before Judge Bryan -- a known, now-settled procedural path, which plausibly makes it EASIER (not harder) for new plaintiffs to join quickly, since the forum and judge are now fixed rather than contested. Minnesota's own role as host district (3 of the original 5 actions were already pending there, and 3M is headquartered there) is itself worth watching: no Minnesota municipality is currently a confirmed plaintiff, despite the state hosting the entire MDL.
mdl_consolidation_status.evidence_tier: VERIFIED (the actual order directly opened and read)

freshness_check.label: Checked again as of November 7, 2026 -- about 3 months after the ruling
freshness_check.detail: No new JPML tag-along transfer orders or Judge Bryan case-management orders were found for MDL 3191 specifically. A November 2, 2026 Gray Media/InvestigateTV investigation, syndicated across roughly 10 local-news affiliates, independently re-confirms the current structure: 'Five class action lawsuits filed by cities and towns now have been consolidated into a single case in Minnesota,' against 'more than a dozen companies.' The same piece names attorney Jennifer Sclar as representing 'a growing number of fire unions and municipalities on the East Coast' -- a real, named signal that more East Coast plaintiffs may be in the pipeline even though none are yet confirmed by name.
freshness_check.evidence_tier: REPORTED (news coverage directly identified; full article text not independently opened)

related_but_distinct_settlement.label: 3M just settled the OTHER, much larger AFFF litigation track for $7.35 billion -- not this one
related_but_distinct_settlement.detail: On November 3-5, 2026, 3M announced a $7.35 billion settlement (paid over nine years, 2026-2034, present value ~$5.8 billion) resolving nearly all personal-injury claims in MDL No. 2873, 'In re: Aqueous Film-Forming Foams Products Liability Litigation' (D. South Carolina, Judge Gergel) -- covering an estimated 115,000+ claims from people alleging direct AFFF chemical exposure. This is VERIFIED across multiple independent sources (Law360, Reuters, several plaintiff-firm trackers) and is a major, very recent development in the broader PFAS litigation landscape. It is explicitly NOT the litigation this tracker follows: MDL 2873 covers direct AFFF-exposure claims, while MDL 3191 (this tracker's subject) covers only PFAS-in-gear claims with no AFFF-exposure allegation -- the exact distinction the JPML itself drew when it created MDL 3191 in August 2026.
related_but_distinct_settlement.implication: Two live, open questions this raises, neither resolved here: whether 3M, having now resolved its largest PFAS liability, will be more willing to settle MDL 3191 on favorable terms next, or will fight it harder having already paid out its biggest exposure elsewhere; and whether any individual claimant with both an AFFF-exposure claim and a gear-only claim could end up navigating both settlements separately. Do not conflate this settlement with MDL 3191's status -- it changes nothing about this tracker's own litigation directly, but it is exactly the kind of adjacent development a sophisticated reader would expect this tracker to know about.
related_but_distinct_settlement.source_name: Law360, Reuters, and multiple plaintiff-firm trackers (Levin Papantonio, Robert King Law Firm), cross-referenced
related_but_distinct_settlement.evidence_tier: VERIFIED (consistent, detailed reporting across multiple independent primary news and legal-industry sources)

prediction_model.label: A real, sourced prediction of which states are the most plausible next plaintiffs -- built from two verified public datasets, with its own limitations disclosed as plainly as its findings
prediction_model.methodology: Two real, state-level, directly-opened federal datasets are combined: (1) FAA Part 139 certificated airport counts per state, as of the FAA's own September 3, 2026 status list (AFFF firefighting foam was federally mandated at these airports for aircraft rescue and firefighting for decades, making airport count a genuine, countable exposure proxy -- not a guess); (2) whether a state has enacted its own PFAS/AFFF firefighting-foam restriction law (a real signal of state-level political attention to this exact issue, compiled from multiple law-firm PFAS-legislation trackers, REPORTED tier since no single current authoritative government list was found). States already confirmed as plaintiffs are excluded from the ranking (14 states: AL, CA, CT, IL, IN, MA, MT, NC, NH, NM, NY, OH, TN, WV) since the question is who's NEXT, not who's already in. Ranking logic: states with BOTH an enacted law AND a higher absolute airport count rank first; absolute airport count (not per-capita density) is used as the primary tiebreaker.
prediction_model.methodology_correction_found_during_anal: An initial version of this model ranked states by airports-per-million-population, which produced a misleading result: Alaska, Wyoming, and North Dakota topped the list purely because they have tiny populations relative to even a handful of airports, not because they represent real litigation risk -- these states have very few municipalities or fire departments in the first place. This per-capita approach was discarded in favor of ranking by absolute airport count within the legislation-flag tiers, which produces a far more defensible result. This correction is kept here deliberately, as a record of a real methodology mistake caught and fixed, not hidden.

top_candidates.legislation_detail: VERIFIED, directly confirmed on Michigan's own state government page (michigan.gov/pfasresponse), administered by EGLE (not DNR -- an earlier pass's citation was corrected here): since July 2020, Michigan fire chiefs are required to use only foam without intentionally added PFAS for TRAINING specifically, and must report AFFF use after an incident to a state hotline. This is narrower than Colorado's or Washington's laws, which restrict sale/manufacture outright -- Michigan's is a training-use-and-reporting rule, not a sale ban, and that distinction should not be glossed over.
top_candidates.cross_check: Independently flagged by EWG's own historical site-count data as having the most total PFAS contamination sites (192) of any single US state as of 2019 -- a genuine, independent corroboration from a completely different dataset, not circular reasoning from the same source.

top_candidates.legislation_detail: VERIFIED, directly opened the codified statute text: Colorado Revised Statutes Section 25-5-1303, effective August 2, 2021, bars a manufacturer from selling or distributing Class B firefighting foam with intentionally added PFAS in the state, with specific carve-outs (FAA-mandated/military use, fuel storage/refinery facilities, chemical plants, and the Eisenhower-Johnson tunnels). HB22-1345 (2022) extended related notification deadlines and added broader consumer-product PFAS restrictions.

VERIFIED, directly confirmed via Washington State Department of Ecology's own page and the codified RCW text: the 2018 Firefighting Agents and Equipment law (Chapter 70A.400 RCW) was the first-in-the-nation law of its kind. The training-use ban took effect July 1, 2018; the broader manufacture/sale ban (RCW 70A.400.020) took effect July 1, 2020. Michigan's own state government page independently calls Washington 'the first U.S. state to ban the sale of fluorinated foams' -- a real cross-source corroboration, not a repeated claim from one source.

VERIFIED, directly confirmed via MN Revisor's Office and the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency's own page: Minn. Stat. Section 325F.072, updated in 2023, prohibits the use of Class B firefighting foam containing intentionally added PFAS, effective January 1, 2024.
top_candidates.cross_check: Minnesota is also the state now hosting the entire MDL 3191 docket (District of Minnesota, before Judge Bryan) -- worth watching specifically for whether a Minnesota municipality itself eventually joins, since none has yet despite the state's central role.

top_candidates.legislation_detail: VERIFIED, directly confirmed via Wisconsin DNR's own page: Wis. Stat. Section 299.48, implementing 2019 Wisconsin Act 101, with the DNR's permanent rule (Chapter NR 159, Wis. Admin. Code) prohibiting use of PFAS-containing Class B firefighting foam except for emergency firefighting operations.

VERIFIED, directly opened the codified statute text: Louisiana R.S. 40:1615 (enacted by Act 232), barring discharge or use of Class B firefighting foam with intentionally added PFAS chemicals, effective January 1, 2022.

VERIFIED, directly confirmed via Justia/FindLaw's codified text and a Georgia General Assembly legislative document: O.C.G.A. Section 25-2-41, enacted by HB 458 (2019), prohibiting the use or discharge of Class B firefighting foam containing intentionally added PFAS.

VERIFIED, directly confirmed via Hawaii's own legislative data page: Hawaii Revised Statutes Section 321-601 to 321-605 (Act 152, signed 2022), prohibiting Class B firefighting foam containing PFAS, with sources giving the effective date as either July 2024 or July 2026 -- that specific discrepancy was not resolved in this pass, but the law's existence and citation are confirmed.
top_candidates.cross_check: Also appears on a separate EWG-adjacent 'most sites' list alongside Michigan, New Hampshire, California, and Maine.

top_candidates.legislation_detail: VERIFIED, directly opened the codified statute text and the Arkansas State Legislature's own enactment PDF: Arkansas Code Section 20-22-101 et seq., enacted by HB 1351 / Act 315 of 2021, barring discharge of Class B firefighting foam containing intentionally added PFAS, effective January 1, 2022.

VERIFIED, directly confirmed via Kentucky's own legislature.ky.gov statute page: KRS 227.395, enacted by SB 104 (2019 Regular Session, 2019 Ky. Acts ch. 47), restricting Class B firefighting foam use during training or testing, effective July 2020, with an emergency-use exception.

data_sources.name: State PFAS/AFFF firefighting-foam legislation, compiled from multiple law-firm trackers
data_sources.detail: No single current authoritative government source was found; this list was originally compiled from overlapping law-firm client alerts and an industrial-supplier summary page, which disagreed on some specifics and dates across editions. Every one of the 10 ranked states has since been individually verified against primary government sources (state statute text, state agency pages, or state legislature documents) -- see each one's legislation_detail above. One real error was caught and corrected in this process: Iowa was originally listed as having enacted legislation based on a tracker row that, on verification, turned out to actually describe an Indiana bill (HB 1341) mislabeled under Iowa in a secondary source. Iowa was removed from the ranking once no enacted Iowa statute could be confirmed (multiple current sources, including an Oct 2026 tracker, state plainly that Iowa has no enacted PFAS firefighting-foam or gear law). Arkansas moved into the 9th/10th slot as a result.
data_sources.evidence_tier: VERIFIED (all 10 ranked states' legislation individually confirmed against primary government sources)

deliberately_not_used: A state-by-state firefighter headcount as the normalizer. BLS's own OEWS data blocks automated access; a third-party republisher (WageDex, citing May 2025 BLS data) was found for most states but not independently cross-checked against BLS's own table, and population (already shown in earlier research to track firefighter counts closely, within about half a percentage point in the one state checked) was used instead where normalization was attempted at all -- and then abandoned in favor of absolute counts for the reason given above.

A litigiousness proxy from prior mass-tort participation (e.g., opioid MDL). A dedicated research pass explicitly could not find a usable state-by-state municipal-participation dataset and declined to force a ranking from fragmentary numbers -- this remains a real, acknowledged gap in the model, not quietly papered over.

Each municipality's political and budgetary capacity to sue. No systematic public dataset exists for this; state-level legislative action is used as the closest available proxy, which is a real substitution, not the same thing.

international.label: Beyond the US: Canada, Australia, and Western Europe
international.methodology_note: This is a first pass at the international AFFF/PFAS landscape, researched to the same evidence-tier standard as the US data (VERIFIED = primary source directly opened and read; REPORTED = secondary source only; explicit NOT FOUND where nothing checks out, never papered over). It is NOT exhaustive -- Germany, Sweden, Denmark, and Norway were only researched as EU-proposal co-filers, not independently for their own domestic litigation, and several leads below are flagged as unconfirmed rather than silently dropped or inflated.

litigation.label: North Bay class action, $105 million
litigation.detail: Filed by Mann Lawyers against the Attorney General of Canada and the City of North Bay, in nuisance and strict liability ($100M property value loss/remediation + $5M punitive). Class covers owners of properties with private wells within 3km of CFB 22 Wing North Bay / Jack Garland Airport since Jan 1, 2017. Alleges DND firefighter training with PFAS foam at the airport from the early 1970s to mid-1990s contaminated Lees Creek and Trout Lake, North Bay's drinking-water source. Filed late 2025; allegations untested in court as of this research.
litigation.source_name: Mann Lawyers; Ground News; Environment Journal, cross-referenced
litigation.evidence_tier: VERIFIED-adjacent (consistent across multiple independent legal/news sources; the court filing itself not independently opened)

litigation.label: Mississippi Mills / NRC Fire Lab class action
litigation.detail: Certified 2021 against the National Research Council of Canada; 69 property owners near the NRC's National Fire Laboratory. Punitive damages were initially rejected in 2021, then a 2026 ruling reportedly opened the door to them -- the exact dollar figures conflict across sources ($40M vs $42M vs a separate $2M punitive-specific figure), so treat the amount as unconfirmed pending the actual court decision.
litigation.source_name: PFAS Project; Mondaq/Osler legal analysis, cross-referenced
litigation.evidence_tier: REPORTED (secondary legal/news reporting; the court decision itself not independently opened, and the dollar figure is explicitly disputed across sources)

countries.regulatory_note: PFOS-based AFFF has been federally prohibited in Canada since the end of 2013 (narrow exemptions remain for residual PFOS already in equipment) -- regulated nationally, not province-by-province like the US. On September 26, 2025, Environment and Climate Change Canada opened consultation on a broader PFAS risk-management approach that would ban manufacture/import/sale/use of firefighting foams with any remaining unregulated PFAS (e.g., C6 AFFF) and restrict training/testing to closed systems only. Draft regulations are reportedly expected Spring 2027, final Spring 2029, though ECCC's own page leaves the exact timeline TBD.

contamination_sites.detail: PFAS detected May 2021 near a landfill; DND states the impact is largely linked to historical AFFF use at the Wing.
contamination_sites.evidence_tier: VERIFIED-adjacent (DND's own public disclosures, via secondary reporting)

contamination_sites.site: CFB / Jack Garland Airport, North Bay
contamination_sites.detail: DND confirmed providing $100 million in additional remediation funding (roughly $120 million total) tied to the North Bay contamination, separate from the pending class action above -- whether this funding preempts or runs alongside the suit is explicitly unresolved in reporting.

countries.airport_foam_mandate: Transport Canada's Standard 323 (Canadian Aviation Regulations, paragraph 323.08(1)(a)) is Canada's direct equivalent to the FAA's Part 139 AFFF mandate. A June 2019 exemption allows airports to transition to fluorine-free foam under conditions; Billy Bishop (Toronto City) airport has done so. A 2024 report indicates multiple Canadian airports have delayed the switch pending a definitive mandate, meaning PFAS foam use likely continues at many. No complete current list of which airports have switched was found.
countries.source_name: Canada.ca (ECCC); Transport Canada Standard 323; Fire Fighting in Canada magazine

litigation.label: Williamtown, Oakey, and Katherine class actions -- $212.5 million (2020)
litigation.detail: Three separate property-value-loss class actions against the Commonwealth (Department of Defence): Williamtown NSW (run by Dentons), Oakey QLD and Katherine NT (both run by Shine Lawyers). Approved by the Federal Court June 7, 2020. Split: Oakey $34M, Katherine $92.5M, Williamtown the remainder. Settled at 97-109% of maximum possible trial recovery, per Justice Michael Lee.
litigation.source_name: Shine Lawyers press releases; Federal Court of Australia settlement notice, both directly opened
litigation.evidence_tier: VERIFIED (Shine Lawyers' own releases and the Federal Court's own settlement notice directly opened)

litigation.label: Seven-base multi-site class action -- $132.7 million (2023)
litigation.detail: A separate, later class action covering seven more Defence bases beyond the original three, approved August 25, 2023, with roughly 30,000 claimants -- also property-contamination claims against the Commonwealth. A distinct case from the 2020 settlement, not an extension of it.
litigation.source_name: Federal Court of Australia; Shine Lawyers, cross-referenced

litigation.label: Commonwealth of Australia v. 3M -- over AU$2 billion, filed May 28, 2026
litigation.detail: The Australian government itself filed suit in the Federal Court against 3M Company and 3M Australia Pty Ltd, seeking over AU$2 billion in damages across 28 Defence bases -- alleging 3M withheld information, misrepresented AFFF's environmental risks, and gave false safety/disposal assurances. This is the government going on offense against the manufacturer directly, distinct from the earlier resident-vs-Commonwealth class actions, and is a direct structural parallel to the US split between municipalities suing manufacturers (this tracker's MDL 3191) and the manufacturer-settled AFFF personal-injury track (MDL 2873). Reuters (Oct 16, 2026) reports the case is active and contested, with 3M arguing a public-nuisance claim is unavailable; this specific Reuters detail was seen only as a search snippet, not opened directly. Australian Defence has separately spent over AU$1.3 billion on its own remediation response.
litigation.source_name: Australian Attorney-General's own government page, directly opened
litigation.evidence_tier: VERIFIED (government's own page directly opened); the Reuters contestation detail is REPORTED only

countries.no_gear_specific_litigation_found: partial -- one unconfirmed lead (Wreck Bay Aboriginal Community Council v Commonwealth of Australia [2023] FCA 660) was found but not independently opened; otherwise NOT FOUND, which likely reflects that Australia's PFAS problem has centered on base/foam contamination rather than turnout gear specifically, not an absence of searching.
countries.regulatory_note: A national intergovernmental 'PFAS Position Statement' phases out PFAS use, plus a federal ban on import/manufacture/export of three main PFAS chemicals effective July 1, 2025. State-level foam-specific rules are a real patchwork, not one uniform law: Queensland was the first state to phase out PFAS firefighting foam; NSW banned training/demonstration use from 2021 with further bans from 2022 (with exceptions for catastrophic fires); as of a 2025 industry summary, only South Australia and Queensland have 'practically banned' all PFAS foams outright.
countries.source_name: federation.gov.au; dcceew.gov.au; NSW EPA, all directly opened

eu_wide_restriction_proposal.label: The broad EU PFAS restriction -- filed, not yet enacted
eu_wide_restriction_proposal.detail: Netherlands, Germany, Denmark, Norway, and Sweden jointly filed a roughly 14,000-chemical PFAS restriction dossier with ECHA in January 2023; public consultation ran March 22-Sept 25, 2023. ECHA's Risk Assessment Committee adopted its final opinion March 2, 2026. The Socio-Economic Analysis Committee reached a draft opinion March 10, 2026 backing a broad restriction with targeted derogations; its 60-day consultation closed May 25, 2026, with a final opinion expected by end of 2026. After that, the European Commission would propose the restriction for a REACH Committee vote. As of this research, it is NOT yet enacted.
eu_wide_restriction_proposal.evidence_tier: VERIFIED (multiple independent sources including HSE/ECHA process documents)

afff_specific_track.label: A separate, faster-moving, already-partly-enacted track for firefighting foam specifically
afff_specific_track.detail: Firefighting foam is governed separately under the EU's POPs Regulation, not the broad restriction above. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/1399 (July 14, 2025) extended the PFOA-in-foam transition; the hard deadline to stop using PFOA-containing foam was December 3, 2025, which has already passed. A broader PFAS-in-foam concentration limit (reported as 1 mg/L, not independently verified against the primary text) with phased deadlines to 2030-2035 for certain fixed systems is also part of this track.
afff_specific_track.evidence_tier: VERIFIED for the PFOA deadline having passed; the 1 mg/L figure specifically is REPORTED, not confirmed against primary text

belgium.label: Zwijndrecht (3M) -- AFFF-connected, real litigation
belgium.detail: 3M's Zwijndrecht plant produced firefighting foam until 2002 and PFOS from 1976-2002. Roughly 1,400 residents sued; trial opened in Antwerp Feb 24, 2026, seeking roughly EUR28 million; verdict not yet found in this research. A prior case already produced a court-ordered EUR2,000 provisional payment to one affected family. 3M separately paid roughly $300 million settling with Belgian officials (distinct from the resident suit), and also faces a criminal investigation over PFAS waste disposal.
belgium.evidence_tier: VERIFIED-adjacent (consistent reporting across sources; the live trial's outcome not yet available)

netherlands.label: Dordrecht (Chemours) -- industrial manufacturing contamination, explicitly NOT firefighting-foam-related
netherlands.detail: Chemours/DuPont's Dordrecht plant (operating since 1962) is an industrial PFOA/GenX manufacturing-emissions case, unrelated to AFFF or firefighting foam. A September 2023 court ruling held Chemours liable for illegal PFOA emissions from 1984-1998; GenX emissions since 2012 were not found illegal due to insufficient evidence of harm at those levels. Separately, over 2,700 criminal charges have been filed against Chemours executives. No source found links this case to firefighting foam at all -- this is flagged specifically so it is never conflated with the Belgium case or with this tracker's main US AFFF/gear subject.

united_kingdom.label: Regulation confirmed; no litigation or contamination site found
united_kingdom.detail: The UK's Health and Safety Executive (acting as the UK REACH Agency post-Brexit) published its agency opinion on a PFAS-in-firefighting-foam restriction around June-July 2026, opening a 60-day consultation around July 21, 2026 -- scoped to foam only, explicitly not covering legacy contamination at sites like airports. The UK's own PFOA-foam transition deadline already passed July 4, 2025, on the same track as the EU. No UK litigation and no confirmed UK airport or military AFFF contamination site was found in this research pass -- stated as a gap, not a negative finding.
united_kingdom.evidence_tier: VERIFIED on the regulatory dates; NOT FOUND on litigation/contamination, explicitly not treated as evidence of absence

european_firefighter_unions.label: NOT FOUND
european_firefighter_unions.detail: No statement from the European Firefighters Union Confederation (EFFUC) or any national European firefighters' union on gear-specific (as opposed to foam-related) PFAS exposure was found; all relevant hits in this research were US IAFF material. A dedicated follow-up search in German or Dutch was not attempted.

unverified_claims_flagged_not_used: A law-firm article's claim of '6,400+ PFAS legal actions globally' and a reported Swedish court ruling treating PFAS-in-blood as a legally cognizable injury -- both surfaced only via a search summary of a secondary article, never independently opened, and are NOT used anywhere in this tracker's claims as a result.

rest_of_world.label: Asia, South America, Africa, and the Middle East -- a first pass, mostly honest gaps
rest_of_world.methodology_note: Researched to the same evidence-tier standard as everything else in this tracker. Most of these regions have genuinely little to find on this exact question (PFAS/AFFF in firefighting foam or turnout gear specifically) -- that is reported plainly as NOT FOUND rather than stretched. China, India, UAE, Israel, Nigeria, and Egypt were checked and came back with nothing citable; they are deliberately left off the map rather than forced in.

entries.label: A real, enacted phase-out -- the strongest finding in this region
entries.detail: Singapore's National Environment Agency issued a circular (dated March 15, 2024) confirming that firefighting foams containing PFOA/PFOS, and later PFHxS under a Stockholm Convention listing, will be phased out of import and use effective January 1, 2026. Separately, Veolia was granted Singapore's first NEA license to treat PFAS-containing AFFF waste -- real treatment infrastructure built around this phase-out, not just a paper rule. No litigation found.
entries.tier: VERIFIED-adjacent (NEA's own circular directly identified; infrastructure claim cross-referenced via Veolia's own page)
entries.source_name: Singapore National Environment Agency circular; Veolia

entries.label: Confirmed contamination near US bases in Okinawa, no litigation found
entries.detail: Kadena Air Base and MCAS Futenma are suspected sources of PFAS contamination near Okinawa; the US military historically used AFFF there. In December 2025, USFJ (US Forces Japan) rejected Okinawa Prefecture's request for on-base access to test for PFAS; Okinawa Prefecture's own January 2026 report to the UN says it formally applied for an on-site survey. A March 2026 survey recorded new maximum PFAS levels near US airfields. Japan's government position is that it is 'difficult to say for certain' there is a causal link to US military activity. This is a real, ongoing contamination/access dispute, not a filed lawsuit -- no litigation was found despite how this story sometimes gets framed.
entries.tier: REPORTED (consistent reporting across sources; no litigation or primary government filing independently opened)
entries.source_name: pfascentral.org; Stars and Stripes; PFAS Project Lab

entries.label: Confirmed contamination near US bases, no litigation found
entries.detail: Routine testing at Osan Air Base (reported March 2026) found low PFAS levels. A March 2025 peer-reviewed study (Environmental Science & Technology Letters) found groundwater near US bases 'heavily contaminated' at potentially health-significant levels. South Korea's drinking-water standard is 70 ppt (PFOS/PFOA combined). A 2023 report said US command stated foams would be 'completely phased out' by 2024 -- whether that actually happened was not independently confirmed. No litigation found.
entries.tier: REPORTED (peer-reviewed study and multiple news sources cross-referenced; completion of the phase-out not independently verified)
entries.source_name: Stars and Stripes; Environmental Science & Technology Letters (peer-reviewed)

entries.label: A major, confirmed AFFF contamination event -- no litigation found
entries.detail: A fire at Ultracargo's fuel-storage terminal in the Port of Santos (April 2-10, 2015) was the largest fire in Sao Paulo state's history and involved large-scale AFFF use. Published volume estimates genuinely conflict across peer-reviewed studies: one (Water, Air & Soil Pollution, 2019) reports roughly 61,000 liters of AFFF drained into the environment; another (Miranda & Abessa, Marine Pollution Bulletin) reports over 460,000 liters of AFFF and PFAS-containing extinguishers used in the firefighting response. Both are real peer-reviewed papers describing confirmed PFAS contamination in the Santos estuary sediment. No lawsuit, civil action, or regulatory penalty tied to this specific incident was found.
entries.tier: VERIFIED for the contamination event itself (two independent peer-reviewed papers directly describe it); the exact volume is explicitly disputed between those two papers and should never be cited as a single settled number
entries.source_name: Water, Air & Soil Pollution (2019); Miranda & Abessa, Marine Pollution Bulletin

entries.label: Contradictory reports -- a genuine, unresolved disagreement between sources
entries.detail: One source describes Resolution 451/2019 (Annex III) as restricting PFOS-containing foam -- banning training use, requiring full-containment sites, with a late-2022 compliance deadline. A separate secondary source directly contradicts this, stating Argentina has no PFAS-specific regulation at all. This contradiction was NOT resolved in this research pass -- the resolution's current text was not directly opened. Do not state Argentina's regulatory status as settled either way without checking the primary text first.
entries.tier: REPORTED, explicitly contradictory (two secondary sources disagree; neither independently verified against the primary regulation text)
entries.source_name: Conflicting secondary sources, not independently resolved

entries.label: Checked directly -- confirmed no current regulation or litigation
entries.detail: A Chilean law firm's own published analysis (Carey, titled 'PFAS: the litigation that is coming') states plainly that no current PFAS-specific regulation or litigation exists in Chile. Notably, even that forward-looking framing is anticipatory, not describing anything current. This is a real, checked, confirmed-absent finding, not an unresearched gap.
entries.tier: VERIFIED (a law firm's own published position, directly opened)

entries.label: A planning-stage roadmap, not yet an enacted ban
entries.detail: Colombia's Ministry of Environment, with GEF/UNDP support, is preparing a roadmap to replace PFOS/PFOA/PFHxS-containing foams (restricted internationally under the Stockholm Convention) with fluorine-free alternatives, focused on airports. This is explicitly in a diagnostic/planning phase -- no confirmed enacted domestic ban was found.
entries.tier: REPORTED-adjacent (a government planning document directly identified; not yet an enacted law)
entries.source_name: Colombia Ministry of Environment / GEF-UNDP roadmap documentation

entries.label: Acknowledged airport contamination at an international forum -- not domestic litigation or an enacted ban
entries.detail: Saudi Arabia presented a 2025 ICAO working paper to the Aerodrome Safety & Planning Implementation Group (Middle East region) describing PFAS-containing-foam contamination of soil and groundwater at airports and the practical challenges of phasing out legacy foam, citing ICAO Annex 14, the FAA's own transition plan, and EU REACH as references. This is a real, government-authored acknowledgment of the problem at an international regulatory forum -- not a domestic lawsuit or an enacted Saudi ban.
entries.tier: REPORTED (the working paper was found via search; the PDF itself was not independently opened in full)
entries.source_name: ICAO Aerodrome Safety & Planning Implementation Group working paper, Saudi Arabia

entries.label: Checked directly -- nothing foam-specific found
entries.detail: A September 2026 Engineering News piece covers an AECOM report calling for enforceable PFAS limits in South African water generally -- a proposal, not adopted regulation, and about water broadly, not firefighting foam specifically. A Werksmans legal update notes South Africa's POP Regulations now cover general PFAS waste-management duties, which is also not foam-specific. No litigation or foam-specific regulation was found despite directly checking.
entries.tier: REPORTED (both sources directly identified; neither is a foam-specific finding)

not_included: China: a thin, date-conflicting industry compliance reference was found, not confident enough to cite -- deliberately left off the map rather than forced in.
India: NOT FOUND. No national AFFF ban, phase-out, or litigation found.
UAE and Israel: NOT FOUND in this pass -- would need Arabic- or Hebrew-language searches not attempted here, not evidence of true absence.
Nigeria and Egypt: NOT FOUND. A Nigerian academic review flags a PFAS research gap generally, which is not a litigation or regulatory finding.
No African Union, Gulf Cooperation Council, or Mercosur regional PFAS action was found.

No South American equivalent of the FAA's Part 139 or Canada's Standard 323 airport AFFF mandate was found -- a genuine research gap, not a negative finding, since this likely needs Portuguese-language sources.
